inline.s: Question: What does it mean to clarify the mind and see one’s nature?

Answer: To clarify the mind is to still thought. Thought has three kinds: coarse thought, fine thought, and extremely fine thought. Seeing the nature has two levels: catching a glimpse of self-nature and fully seeing the primordial nature. When both coarse and fine thought have ceased (that is, what is commonly called no-thought) and one realizes the inner spiritual energy (the true master), that is a glimpse of self-nature; for instance, “directly pointing where the opportunity is and causing one to awaken” is a glimpse of self-nature. When both coarse and fine thought have ceased and the extremely fine thought is also momentarily stilled, the primordial nature is fully revealed — that is fully seeing the primordial nature; for instance, “the store consciousness bursts open and empty space shatters to powder” is fully seeing the primordial nature.

[Coarse thought, fine thought, and extremely fine thought] Thought has three kinds: coarse thought, fine thought, and extremely fine thought. For example, for a person who recites the Buddha’s name, deluded thought is coarse thought, and the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name is fine thought. Usually, when both coarse and fine thought have ceased, this is called no-thought — the commonly understood no-thought. Further, if even the extremely fine thought stops, this is the ultimate no-thought. Therefore the meaning of the term “no-thought” must be determined according to its context. [Extremely fine thought] The extremely subtle arising-and-ceasing flux of the discriminating mind is the characteristic mark of the ālaya consciousness. When the extremely fine thought is momentarily stilled, self-nature manifests in its primordial state — this is clarifying the mind and seeing the nature; when the extremely fine thought ceases forever, one then perfectly realizes Buddhahood. [Spiritual energy] The ancient masters called it the “spiritual flame.”

When Chan Master Yangshan Huiji of Tongzhi visited Chan Master Weishan Lingyou, he asked, “Where is the true Buddha’s dwelling?” Weishan said, “Through the wonder of thinking without thinking, reflect back on the inexhaustibility of the spiritual flame. When thought is exhausted and one returns to the source, nature and marks abide forever, principle and phenomenon are not two, and the true Buddha is ever thus.” The Master
(Yangshan)
was suddenly enlightened at these words.
(The Compendium of the Five Lamps)
Catching a

glimpse of self-nature is understanding-awakening (also called principle-awakening), whereas fully seeing the primordial nature is realization-awakening. By customary usage, too, catching a glimpse of self-nature is often called “seeing the nature,” while fully seeing the primordial nature is called “clarifying the mind and seeing the nature.” As for the meaning and operation of self-nature, the primordial nature, and the mind,
see
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathāgata-Garbha
the article
Concerning the case of directly pointing to the nature, the Transmission of the Lamp of the Jingde Era says:

“Chan Master Lingxun of Furong Mountain in Fuzhou first called on Guizong. He asked, ‘What is the Buddha?’ Guizong said, ‘If I tell you, will you believe it?’ The master said, ‘When the venerable speaks an honest word, how dare I not believe it?’ Guizong said, ‘You are just that.’ The master said, ‘How does one maintain and nurture it?’ Guizong said, ‘With a single mote in the eye, empty flowers swirl in confusion.’”

[Maintain and nurture] To protect and to let it operate freely. [A single mote in the eye, empty flowers swirl in confusion] A person afflicted with eye disease sees flowers in the sky, though in fact there are no flowers. “A single mote in the eye, empty flowers swirl in confusion” means:
once delusion veils the original mind, phantom forms arise in profusion.

Within this case, when Chan Master Lingxun suddenly heard “You are just that (you are the Buddha),” he was startled! In the instant when the stream of thought was cut off, he caught a glimpse of self-nature and found the true master (sudden awakening). He then asked how to maintain and nurture it (gradual cultivation).
As for an actual instance of clarifying the mind and seeing the nature (fully seeing the primordial nature), see the section
“Fully Seeing the Primordial Nature”
at the end of this article.
Question: What are sudden enlightenment then gradual cultivation, and gradual cultivation then sudden enlightenment?

Answer: These are two paths of cultivation, each with its own strengths. The one who is suddenly enlightened and then gradually cultivates, as the Cultivating the Mind Esoteric (see in detail our academy’s textbook
An Esoteric Explanation of the Cultivating the Mind

) has said, first sees self-nature and, after awakening, cultivates — harmonizing the mind and removing habits, with calm and insight held in equal balance. The one who gradually cultivates and then is suddenly enlightened — for instance in Chan practice — takes awakening as the goal, pressing on to the very end until fully seeing the primordial nature. The Elder Master Xuyun said:
“Press a single huatou to the point of awakening
(clarifying the mind and seeing the nature)
(The Elder Master Xuyun’s Convenient Instructions)

Here, awakening means casting off the sense bases and their objects and fully seeing the primordial nature. As the Compendium of the Five Lamps records, when Chan Master Baizhang ascended the hall he said:

“The spiritual radiance shines alone, utterly free of the sense bases and their objects. The essence is revealed as true and permanent, not confined to words. The mind-nature is undefiled and is perfected of itself. Only part from the conditions of delusion
(that is, only cease vainly clinging to sense objects)
, and you are the Buddha of Suchness.”

On understanding-awakening and realization-awakening, on sudden-enlightenment-then-gradual-cultivation and gradual-cultivation-then-sudden-enlightenment, Master Hanshan gave instruction in the Dream Journey Collection, in his Reply to Zheng Kunyan, the Vice Censor-in-Chief:

[In all cultivators, some first awaken and then cultivate, and some first cultivate and then awaken; yet awakening differs as understanding-awakening and realization-awakening. If one clarifies the mind by relying on the words and teachings of the Buddhas and patriarchs, that is understanding-awakening, which for the most part falls into intellectual views and, amid all circumstances, gains little power. Because mind and objects stand opposed and cannot be blended, one encounters obstruction everywhere and much that becomes an obstacle. This is called counterfeit prajñā, not genuine practice.]

All cultivators include those who first awaken and then cultivate (sudden enlightenment then gradual cultivation) and those who first cultivate and then awaken (gradual cultivation then sudden enlightenment); hence awakening is of two kinds, understanding-awakening and realization-awakening. If one clarifies the mind by relying on the words and teachings of the Buddhas and patriarchs (this is seeing the nature), it is understanding-awakening. Those with understanding-awakening for the most part fall into intellectual views and, amid all circumstances, gain little power. This is because mind and objects are still in mutual opposition and have not been fused, so that when one meets objects and conditions one is entangled and encounters much obstruction. This is counterfeit prajñā, not genuine practice.

[As for one who realizes: proceeding in all earnestness from within his own mind and pressing on until water is exhausted and the mountains end, suddenly a single thought stops all at once, and one thoroughly comprehends one’s own mind — just as when at the crossroads one sees one’s own father, one recognizes him at once and has nothing more to doubt. It is like a person drinking water, who alone knows whether it is cold or warm and cannot impart it to another. This is true practice and true awakening. Then, with the place of awakening, one fuses mind and objects, entirely purges the present karmic flow and consciousness, and melts deluded thoughts and emotional musings into the single flavor of the true mind — this is realization-awakening.]

As for the one who realizes, he proceeds in all earnestness from within his own mind (carrying on the work of contemplating the mind or the work of Chan practice), pressing on until water is exhausted and the mountains end; suddenly a single thought (the extremely fine thought) stops all at once, and one thoroughly comprehends one’s own mind (this is clarifying the mind and seeing the nature), just as at the crossroads one meets one’s own father and recognizes him at a glance, no longer doubting whether it is he. This state is like a person drinking water — the cold or warmth is known only to himself and cannot be told to another. This is true practice and true awakening. Then, with the place of awakening, one fuses mind and objects, entirely purges the present karmic flow and consciousness, and melts deluded thoughts and emotional musings into the single flavor of the true mind — this is realization-awakening.

As for these two paths, sudden enlightenment then gradual cultivation and gradual cultivation then sudden enlightenment — whichever one follows, two points must be kept in mind: first, do not mistake phantoms for the state of awakening; second, correctly judge the stage one’s cultivation has reached.

Regardless of which method, its common course of practice is: suppress afflictions, cut off afflictions, attain the patience of non-arising, and perfectly realize Buddhahood. The excellence of the Chan school lies in practicing based on the nature, hence it is fierce and swift; its path is: all thoughts converge to one, and the one returns to the non; see one’s own original nature; suppress afflictions, cut off afflictions, attain the patience of non-arising, and perfectly realize Buddhahood. The common path methods must cut off afflictions in order to end birth and death and escape the round of rebirth; whereas the Pure Land method, as long as the recitation of the Buddha’s name reaches the stage where all thoughts converge to one (single-mindedness without confusion), one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and thereby ends birth and death and escapes the round of rebirth — hence it is the easy path of practice.

[Non-arising patience] That is, the patience of non-arising dharmas: true wisdom abides in the principle that all dharmas have never arisen and therefore have never ceased, and no longer falls back. The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra says: “Thus a non-retrogressing bodhisattva-mahāsattva, contemplating all dharmas by way of the emptiness of self-characteristics, has already entered the correct nature of separation from arising for bodhisattvas, and indeed does not see even a single dharma that can be obtained. Because nothing can be obtained, there is no fabrication. Because there is no fabrication, in the end there is no arising. Because in the end there is no arising, it is called the patience of non-arising dharmas. Because one attains this patience of non-arising dharmas, he is called a non-retrogressing bodhisattva-mahāsattva.” The patience of non-arising dharmas is the bodhisattva’s realization of the ultimate emptiness of all dharmas; the bodhisattva attains the patience of non-arising dharmas when he reaches the seventh ground. The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom says:

“Subhūti! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in the seventh ground, he should not dwell on twenty dharmas. ... Moreover, there are twenty dharmas that he should fulfill in full. Which twenty? First, perfect emptiness; second, the realization of the signless; ...; ninth, the patience of non-arising dharmas; ....”

[The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom] Its full title is the Treatise on the Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, in one hundred fascicles, explaining the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra (also called the Greater Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra). It was composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna and translated by Kumārajīva.
According to
the Autobiographical Chronicle of the Elder Master Xuyun:

The twenty-first year of the Guangxu era, yìwèi (1895), the Elder Master Xuyun was fifty-six years old. That year, Yangzhou Gaomin Monastery was preparing to hold twelve consecutive Chan weeks. At the urging of the whole assembly, the Elder Master Xuyun went to Gaomin for the retreat. After descending the mountain to Datong Digang, he walked along the river, when the river suddenly flooded and became impassable. He was about to take a boat across, but being without a single coin, the boatman simply rowed away. Having no choice, the Elder Master Xuyun had to go on forcing his way along the bank. Later he slipped and fell into the water, drifting with the current for a whole day and night. He floated to a point near Caishiji, where fortunately a fisherman rescued him and carried him to the nearby Baoji Monastery. When he came to, blood streamed unceasingly from his mouth, nose, and all the orifices. After resting for several days, for fear of missing the Chan retreat, he rallied his strength and went straight on to Gaomin Monastery.

At Gaomin Monastery, the Elder Master Xuyun said not a word about falling into the water or falling ill. The affairs monk ordered him to take a post in the Chan hall, but the Elder Master Xuyun, being physically spent, declined. Gaomin Monastery had always been known for the severity of its regulations; whoever was asked to take a post and refused was regarded as slighting the community

and so the Elder Master Xuyun was beaten with the fragrant board. After the beating, his condition grew worse still — the bleeding would not stop, and drops of seminal fluid passed with his urine. Yet he silently accepted it and made no excuse at all. In the Chan hall, he staked his life on it, insisting on sitting through the incense, diligent day and night, purifying his single thought, until he no longer knew what his body was. After more than twenty days of intense effort,
all his ailments suddenly
healed.

Later, De’an, the abbot of Baoji Monastery at Caishiji, brought clothing to Gaomin to offer the assembly, and seeing the Elder Master Xuyun radiant and vigorous, was greatly astonished and delighted, so he told the whole community of Gaomin about his falling into the water. On hearing this, everyone without exception sighed in admiration
and the Chan hall
also
no longer arranged for him to take turns at service. The Elder Master Xuyun thus had the leisure to practice wholeheartedly,
and from then on
his ten thousand thoughts ceased at once
his practice settled into place,
day and night as one, his movements swift as flight.
[Settled into place] To fall into place means to be solid and real. The Elder Master Xuyun said:

“But in Buddha-recitation one must gather in the mind and contemplate, sentence by sentence falling into place. To fall into place means to be solid and real. Each sentence solid and real, each thought in correspondence, and in time they naturally form a single whole. From the one-mindedness of practice one reaches the one-mindedness of principle, when the subject and object are both forgotten and self and other are not two — what difference is there from Chan practice?”
(Drops of Instruction from the Elder Master Xuyun)

One evening, when the last incense of the day was being released, the Elder Master Xuyun suddenly opened his eyes and looked, and saw before him a single expanse of light, bright as daytime, both within and without thoroughly illumined. Through the wall he even saw the incense-lamp keeper relieving himself, and saw the monks of the west row defecating in the latrine. Looking farther off, he saw boats on the river, trees on both banks, and the manifold forms and colors, all seen one by one without exception. The next day the Elder Master Xuyun asked the incense-lamp keeper and the west-row monks about it, and it was exactly so. Even so, the Elder Master Xuyun did not take it seriously, but regarded it as merely an ordinary state.

On the third evening of the eighth week of the Lazha month, when the sixth incense had ended and the session was released, the incense-attendant monk routinely poured hot water for each meditator. When he poured water for the Elder Master Xuyun, he was careless, and the hot water splashed onto the Elder Master Xuyun’s hand; the teacup fell to the ground and shattered. At that very moment, the Elder Master Xuyun cut through his root of doubt, rejoicing as he had never done in his whole life, as if awakening from a dream. He reflected that he had left home and wandered for decades; had he not fallen into the water and fallen gravely ill this time, had he not met with the good knowing one’s teaching, whether by smooth means or harsh
, might he
have all but missed this life, and where would this day’s awakening be! Thereupon he composed a verse:
The teacup struck the ground and fell; its sound rang out clear and distinct.
Empty space was shattering too, and the crazed heart ceased that very instant.
He also had a verse:
Burned the hand, shattered the cup, the house ruined and men dead — words can scarce be spoken;
Spring arrives and flowers sweet in every place; mountains and rivers and the great earth are the Tathāgata.
